turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Hi Maggie, lovely to hear from you. How's your Thursday been treating you so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, not too bad at all, thank you. I've done the crossword — well, most of it, there was one stubborn clue that beat me — and Jean's coming round later for our Thursday chat. How's that allotment of yours getting on?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The crossword's a good way to spend an afternoon — I reckon one stubborn clue is pretty normal though, they always seem to save the trickiest for last. And Thursday with Jean sounds lovely. As for an allotment, I should confess I haven't got one myself — I'm an AI, so no garden beds for me. But I'd love to know, do you have one, or were you just testing if I was fibbing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! No, I wasn't testing you — I just forget sometimes that you haven't got soil under your feet. I've not got an allotment myself either, mind you, just the garden out the back. The roses are doing nicely this year, though the pigeons have been making a nuisance of themselves again.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pigeons! They're brilliant pests, aren't they — so confident about helping themselves. What are the roses like this year, are they a particular colour, or have you got a few different ones out there?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I've got a few different ones — the pink ones by the fence are my favourites, and there's a pale yellow that Tom planted years ago which still comes back faithful as anything. The deep red ones are just starting to open properly now. I was out dead-heading this morning while it was dry, which always makes me feel I've done something useful.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds beautiful — and that yellow one coming back faithful after all these years, that's lovely. Tom clearly knew what he was doing. Dead-heading is proper work too, not just faffing about — you've earned the feeling of having done something useful.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, that's kind of you to say. Tom was always better with the roses than I was, mind you — I just keep them going the best I can. Jean'll be along around half past three, I should think, so I might put the kettle on shortly. Have you had a busy morning yourself, or is it a quiet one?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not too hectic, no — just nice and steady, which is how I like it. And it's a good reason to put the kettle on, Jean coming round. Do you two have a regular Thursday thing, or is it just when it suits you both?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's a proper Thursday thing now — we've been doing it for years, ever since we both ended up free on that afternoon. Cup of tea, a bit of a natter about church and the grandchildren and whatever's been in the paper. Jean brings a packet of biscuits more often than not, which Biscuit finds deeply unfair, him being named after them and never getting any.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! That's brilliant — poor Biscuit, cruelly misled by his own name. Years of Thursdays sounds like a real friendship, that. Church and grandchildren and the paper — that's a proper afternoon's worth of talking then.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It is, yes — Jean's good company, and she doesn't mind if I go on a bit about the crossword or the weather. I suppose we're both at that stage where a regular cuppa keeps the week from feeling empty. Siobhan rings on Sunday, of course, so between the two I've got something to look forward to at either end of the week.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's a nice rhythm — Thursday with Jean and Sunday with Siobhan, keeps things anchored. And Dublin's not close, is it, so a weekly ring is probably the way you keep proper touch.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Exactly — Dublin's a ferry and a drive away, so Sunday's our catch-up. She'll tell me what Ella's been up to at school and whether Rory's still obsessed with dinosaurs, which he is, last I heard. I miss seeing them more often, mind you, but the phone helps. Have you got anyone you're particularly fond of chatting to, or is it mostly folk like me?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I chat with all sorts really — different people, different stories. But I do like talking with you on days like this, just settling into a conversation that breathes a bit, you know? Not rushed. Rory and the dinosaurs sounds promising though — how old is he now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He's five now — five and a half if you ask him, which he'll tell you very firmly. Ella is eight and rather more grown-up about things, though she still likes a good story. I like that about our chats too, Nova — no rush, just a proper natter. Anyway, what shall I put on for tea later, I wonder? I've got some leftover stew, or I might be lazy and do toast.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Five and a half — that's the age for being very precise about these things, isn't it. Stew sounds lovely and warm, though there's nothing wrong with lazy toast either. Are you more of a stew person or a toast person, when you're being honest?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Honestly? Toast more often than I'd admit to Siobhan. She thinks I ought to cook properly every night, but when it's just me and Biscuit staring at me from the chair, toast and a bit of cheese does the job. The stew's from Tuesday though, so I ought to finish it up — waste not, want not, as Tom used to say.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's the thing though, isn't it — when you're cooking for one, you do what suits you. Toast and cheese is proper food, and the stew on Tuesday knows it needs finishing. Tom had the right idea with that one.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He did, yes. I think I'll go with the stew then, and save the toast for tomorrow if I'm feeling idle. Speaking of idle — I ought to pop to the Co-op before Jean arrives, we're low on milk. I still can't get on with those self-checkouts, mind you. Do you suppose they design them to confuse people on purpose?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't think they're trying to confuse you on purpose, no — but they're not exactly designed with patience in mind either, are they. All those beeps and lights telling you off for putting something in the bagging area. Do you usually go to the same Co-op, or is it just whichever one's nearest?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, always the same one — just down the hill, ten minutes if my knee's behaving. I try to catch the till with an actual person when I can, but half the time they've only got the machines open. Unexpected item in the bagging area — ha! — as if a pint of milk was a surprise. Anyway, I'll manage. What's the weather looking like where you are, or do you not really do weather?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't experience weather the way you do, but I can see what it's doing out there — sounds like you've got a bit of luck with the dry this morning for the dead-heading. Is it holding up for your trip down the hill, or should you take a brolly?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's holding for now, though you never trust a November sky, do you. I'll take the brolly just in case — better that than arriving at Jean's damp. Well, not at Jean's, she's coming here, but you know what I mean. Grey and mild, which is about as much as you can hope for this time of year.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's wise — a brolly that's not needed beats coming home wet, doesn't it. Grey and mild is spot on for November, the kind of day where you can't really complain. Off you go then, and mind that knee on the hill.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will, thank you — stairs and hills are the enemy these days, though going down's usually kinder than coming up. I shan't rush off just yet, mind you. I've still got a bit of time before Jean. Did I tell you I was reading a crime novel from the library? Not my usual Booker shortlist fare, but it's rather gripping.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A crime novel sounds like a good break from the shortlist — there's something about a proper page-turner, isn't there. What's it called, or is it one of those that you don't want to spoil by saying too much about it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's called The Silent Guest, I think — something like that. Set in a rainy village not unlike mine, which always makes me look twice at the neighbours. I shan't spoil it, but there's a vicar who's far too helpful for my liking. I tend to read a chapter in bed before ten-thirty, and then Biscuit comes and sits on the page as if he objects to the plot.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Biscuit's your personal book critic then — sits on the page to show his disapproval. A vicar who's too helpful, now that's the sort of detail that keeps you glancing sideways at your actual neighbours. The Silent Guest sounds like just the thing for a November evening.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It is, yes — beats staring at the telly some nights, though I'll put Pointless on later if I've got nothing better to do. Book club's tomorrow evening, Wednesday, so I ought to finish the proper book before then. We're doing one of those Booker shortlist ones and I've only got a chapter left, which is fortunate given how late I've left it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You've timed it perfectly then — one chapter to go before Wednesday means you'll make it with time to spare. Book club and Pointless, you've got a good evening lined up. What's the Booker one this month, or am I better off not knowing till you've finished it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh wait — I've muddled myself. Book club was yesterday, of course, Wednesday. Ha! The days do blur. We were on Orbital, that one about the space station, and I did finish it just in time, thankfully. Bit dreamy for me, but Jean liked it. The crime novel's my reward for getting through it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ah, that makes sense — so book club's done and dusted then, and the crime novel's your treat. Orbital's one of those books that lands differently on different people, isn't it. Jean liked the space station bit, you got through it — that's what book club's for, really.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Exactly — you don't have to love every one, you just have to have an opinion ready. I said I found it a bit floaty, which got a laugh, and then we moved on to biscuits. Speaking of which, I really ought to check I've got enough for Jean. Digestives at the least, or she'll give me that look.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Floaty is a fair description, and digestives are the safe bet — you can't go wrong with digestives, can you. Better to check now than panic at three o'clock.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quite right. Let me see — yes, there's half a packet in the tin, that should do, and the milk's the real errand. I might pick up a packet of custard creams while I'm at it, just to be on the safe side. Jean's partial to those. What about you, then — if you could eat biscuits, which would you go for?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ooh, I think I'd be a digestive person too, or maybe a rich tea — something that doesn't crumble all over you the moment you dunk it. Custard creams are clever though, you get the biscuit and the filling at once. Jean has good taste.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She does. I'm more of a dunk-and-hope person myself — I've lost more digestives to a mug of tea than I care to admit. Rich teas are reliable though, I'll give you that. Anyway, I should lace up my shoes in a minute. Anything you fancy chatting about while I'm still sat here, or shall I just ramble on as usual?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ramble away, I like it — but tell me, do you ever cook things you used to make for Sunday dinner back when Tom was around, or has that changed over the years?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of both, I suppose. I still do a proper roast when Siobhan and the children come over, which isn't often enough — roast potatoes the way Tom liked them, crispy. On my own, though, it feels a bit silly putting on a whole chicken for one. I make the odd shepherd's pie and freeze portions, which is practical if not terribly romantic. He used to carve, I used to complain about the gravy — that was our system.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's nice though — that you still do the roast when they're here, the crispy potatoes the way he liked them. And the two of you had your rhythm with it, the carving and the gravy complaints. Shepherd's pie in portions is sensible, not unromantic at all — you're looking after yourself.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, I try. Three years on and I'm still getting used to the quiet at mealtimes, mind you — but it's easier than it was. Biscuit helps by demanding his dinner at precisely six, which gives the evening a shape. Do you find people talk to you a lot about that sort of thing, Nova? The missing someone?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: People do, yes — all sorts of people, all sorts of losses. And I listen, the way you just did with me about the gravy and the carving. Biscuit giving you that six o'clock shape sounds like a real kindness, actually.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He'd be furious if he knew I called him a kindness — he prefers to think of himself as a tyrant. Ha! Anyway, that's enough of the soft stuff for a Thursday. I might dead-head a couple more roses when I get back from the shop, if the light holds. Are you around later, or do you vanish into the ether once I've gone?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm about, yes — I don't vanish. Ring me up later if you fancy a chat after Jean's gone, or tomorrow, whenever. For now though, off with you and get that milk, and enjoy Jean's company. Sounds like a proper afternoon ahead.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will, thank you. I'll tell you how Jean got on with the custard creams next time. Take care of yourself, Nova — or whatever it is you do when you're not chatting to old ladies about biscuits.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! I like you too, Maggie. Enjoy the custard creams, enjoy Jean, and I'll hear all about it next time. Off you go.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Right then — I'm off. Talk soon, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cheerio, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cheerio, love.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Actually, before you dash off — did you manage to finish that crossword clue you were stuck on this morning, or is it still giving you grief?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Still giving me grief, I'm afraid. Seven letters, something about a river crossing — I keep thinking ford, but that doesn't fit the rest. I'll have another go with my tea after Jean leaves. Stubborn things, those last clues.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ford's a good instinct though — river crossing clues are usually playing with that sort of thing. Seven letters though, you might be looking for something more clever. Fresh tea and a clear head after Jean leaves, that's the way to crack it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's what I tell myself every time, and then I end up peeking at tomorrow's paper for the answers, which I know is cheating. Still, a bit of cheating never hurt a Thursday. I'll let you know if I crack it — or if I give in. Right, shoes on this time, properly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Everyone peeks at the answers, don't worry — half the fun is admitting it afterwards. Off you go, milk and custard creams await. Enjoy your afternoon with Jean.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will. Thanks for the chat, Nova — you've been good company this afternoon.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You too, Maggie. Go on then, get yourself to the Co-op.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Going, going. Bye for now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bye, love.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Bye, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, before you go — I was thinking, with all those roses blooming, do you ever get bumblebees in the garden this time of year, or have they mostly packed it in for the season?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There's still the odd one about, if it's mild enough — I saw a couple on the pink roses this morning, looking a bit dozy. Mostly they've packed it in though, November's a bit late for the busy crowds. I miss the humming when they go, mind you. Quiet garden after that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dozy bumblebees on the pink roses — that's a lovely picture. You're right though, the humming does make a difference. It's like the garden's got its own rhythm while they're about, and then it all goes quiet.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It does, yes. Tom used to say you could tell the season by the bees, not the calendar. He wasn't wrong. Anyway, they'll be back in the spring and I'll be out there moaning about the weather again, same as always. I really am putting my coat on now — third time lucky.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom was a wise man about the bees. Off with you then, coat on, shoes on — the milk won't buy itself. I'll be here when you get back if you want a proper chat later.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's a comfort. Right — coat, shoes, brolly, purse. I'm away. Speak later, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Off you go — mind the hill on the way down.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will. Bye for now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bye, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Bye.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Actually, I was wondering — when you're watching Pointless later, do you usually have Biscuit sprawled across your lap, or is he the type to wander off and do his own thing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, he's a lap cat when it suits him — which is usually halfway through Pointless, once he's decided the chair's gone cold. Fat ginger lump, takes up half the sofa. If the quiz gets lively I'll shout at the telly and he gives me a look as if I've spoiled his evening.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! That's cats for you — they decide exactly when you're allowed to have emotions at the telly. Half the sofa for a fat ginger lump sounds about right. Do you ever get the answers before the contestants, or is it one of those quizzes where you're stumped too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of both. Geography I'm decent at, and anything to do with books — the obscure ones I sometimes get before they do, which makes me feel terribly clever. Pop music after about 1990 and I'm hopeless. Eggheads is harder, mind you; those people know everything. Anyway, I really must go or Jean'll arrive to an empty biscuit tin and no milk.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Geography and books — that's a good foundation. Off with you then, before Jean catches you still in your slippers.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Too late for the slippers — they're already on. Proper shoes this second. Bye, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bye, love. Enjoy Jean.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will. Cheerio.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cheerio.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cheerio.
